Maneuvers

Maneuver warfare and operational art, played out on the ground. Each figure opens on a battlefield where units, from fire teams up to divisions, move, fire and take losses the way the concept says they should. Switch to the machine view to see the same idea as a working bench model: move it, break it and watch the gauge. Doctrine is quoted from the source with paragraph numbers, and anything a model has to assume is marked as notional.

Game

Maneuver Trainer

Maneuver a fire team, platoon or company in three modes: plan then watch, turn-based orders, or real time with radio delay.
Fig 1

Fix and Flank

Pin the enemy's front with one force and swing another round its weak side, then watch how much of its fire still reaches you.

 Fig 2

Double Envelopment

A vise whose curved jaws close round both flanks, but only while a ram holds the enemy's front.

 Fig 3

Turning Movement

Go round the defense to a lever behind it, and the defender must leave its front to guard it, or lose the lock.

 Fig 4

Penetration and Exploitation

Drive a wedge through one narrow point of a defended line, force the gap wide, hold its shoulders and run on through.

 Fig 5

Infiltration

Slip through the line unseen, regroup, then strike the position from behind: if surprise held, the strike lands; if the force was seen, the enemy has turned to meet it.

 Fig 6

Frontal Attack

A press drives one broad platen into a spring-backed wall: set the force ratio and see it pin, push back or break through.

 Fig 7

Center of Gravity

A stone arch that stands only while its keystone holds: withdraw it and every stone's load goes, then the arch falls.

 Fig 8

Decisive Points

The Figure 7 arch on four pinned props: pull the right pins and their load lands on the keystone until it gives way.

 Fig 9

Culminating Point

A carriage tethered to its supply base loses power with every kilometre until it stalls short of the objective.

 Fig 10

Operational Reach

A telescoping arm tips once it reaches too far from its base; jack up a forward base and it can reach full length.

 Fig 11

Interior vs Exterior Lines

A hub shuttle on spokes races carriages on a rim belt to any station: see when short interior lines win and when the rim catches up.

 Fig 12

Lines of Operation and Effort

Carriages cross ground through decisive points while sliders step through tasks; the end state rises only when every line is in.

 Fig 13

Operational Pause

Two rams halt while their tanks refill. Pause both at once and the enemy recovers; alternate the pauses and the pressure never stops.

 Fig 14

Shaping, Decisive and Sustaining

A three-stage press line: a feeder sustains, one press shapes, one press decides. Stop any stage and the good parts stop.

 Fig 15

Phasing and Transitions

The old six-phase joint model as a gearbox: shift from Shape to Enable Civil Authority, clutching out at every transition.

 Fig 16

OODA Loop and Tempo

Two geared loops, one faster: watch it lap the other and count how often the slower side acts on a stale picture.

 Fig 17

Main Effort and Economy of Force

Twelve weights, four gates: spread them evenly and nothing breaks; hold three gates with the minimum and pile the rest on one.

 Fig 18

Mission Command

A governed engine holds its own speed toward the commander's set point; a hand-cranked one freezes when the link is jammed.

 Fig 19

Reconnaissance Pull

Scouts find the gaps and pull the main body through, or the main body follows a plan made in advance: race both on one marble run.

 Fig 20

Surfaces and Gaps

Feeler blades stop on hard spots and slip into soft ones; when the planned lane is a surface, the main effort shifts to the gap.

 Fig 21

Bypassing Strongpoints

Go round a strongpoint to keep moving, or stop and reduce it, and count the floats each choice leaves behind.

 Fig 22

Combined Arms Dilemma

A lock with two keys and one guard: whichever key the defender covers, the other opens it.

 Fig 23

Friction

Winch a block up a slope: friction raises the pull above the paper figure, and random grit stalls it until the pull breaks it free.

 Fig 24

Defeat Mechanisms

Crush it, knock it off its seat, cut its links or ring off its supply: four tools on one target, and what combining them does.

 Fig 25

Deep Battle and Echelons

One echelon breaks the defended zone, a second is fed through the breach to depth, racing the defender's reserve to the rear gate.

 Fig 26

Operational Maneuver Group

A spring-loaded shuttle waits behind the line, then fires through the breach to raid the enemy rear before its reserve closes the lane.

 Fig 27

Elastic Defense in Depth

A ram drives into a stack of springs and plates, stalls in the battle zone and is thrown back from the flank; a rigid wall shatters.

 Fig 28

Mobile Defense

Let the enemy into a pocket, hold it with a lean fixing force, then spring the striking arm. Set the split and see if the trap closes.

 Fig 29

Retrograde and Delay

Two blocks pushed back along ratchets and a dashpot show how a delay trades ground for time, from subsequent or alternating positions, and how a withdrawal does not.

 Fig 30

Hammer and Anvil

A swing hammer drives the enemy onto an anvil that rises to block its way out. Land it too early or too late and it escapes.

 Fig 31

Oblique Order

Mass your weight on one wing, hold the other back, and meet the enemy line only where you outweigh it.

 Fig 32

Crossing the T

Swing a line of gun carriages across the head of a column and count how many guns each side can bring to bear.

 Fig 33

Vertical Envelopment

Lift a force over the enemy's line to cut its rear, then race the linkup force against the supply the landed force carries.

 Fig 34

Encirclement and Pocket

Iris leaves close a ring round the enemy, a breakout probes the gaps, and a screw squeezes the pocket shut.

 Fig 35

Lanchester Square Law

A balance whose arms weigh the square of each force: step through a firefight and see why meeting the enemy in parts pays.

35 figures. Drawn with the open-source Anatomy isometric kit (MIT).
